system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2161-12-13 16:20:00 to 2161-12-14 19:45:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with a history of tracheobronchomalacia, bronchopulmonary dysplasia, and chronic bronchitis was admitted for increased green, blood-streaked tracheal secretions, dyspnea, substernal burning, and subjective fevers. She was evaluated for possible tracheitis or pneumonia. A bronchoscopy revealed erythema and suspicious plaques; cultures grew Moraxella catarrhalis and a pan-sensitive gram-negative rod (Proteus). She was treated with oral levofloxacin for presumed bacterial tracheitis. Her symptoms improved with antibiotics, nebulized bronchodilators, and supportive care. GERD and depression were managed with home medications. Iron supplementation was discontinued as her anemia remained stable. She was discharged home with follow-up instructions and a five-day course of antibiotics.
problems: Obstructive chronic bronchitis with acute bronchitis

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve been having a lot more mucus from my trach again—greenish, thick—and it’s hard to clear even with suctioning. I’ve also been short of breath, especially at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. This sounds similar to what you had a few days ago. Any fevers this time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fevers, but I’ve had chills and some nausea. And a kind of chest tightness when I can’t clear my airway.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. In the ER, they gave you a dose of ceftriaxone and Zofran for nausea. Your vitals are stable now—heart rate a bit high, but oxygen levels are good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad the oxygen’s okay. But I’m worried—why is this happening again so soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your history of tracheobronchomalacia and recent infection, it’s likely a flare-up—possibly tracheitis again. We’re treating it as a bacterial infection for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was on levofloxacin before, but my pulmonologist told me to stop it. I’ve been on cefuroxime and fluconazole since.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we know. The fluconazole was for possible candidiasis because of the white plaques seen before. We’re continuing that, but switching antibiotics to IV ceftriaxone to cover bacteria more effectively.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the IV antibiotic going to make a difference?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, IV antibiotics get into your system faster and at higher levels. Since you’re not improving with oral meds, this gives us a better chance to clear the infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. What about the chest pain I’ve been having?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It sounds like it’s related to straining to clear secretions. Your lungs are clear on exam, and the chest X-ray shows no pneumonia or other acute issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that’s a relief. I was worried it might be something serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring everything closely. Your labs came back—white blood cell count is normal, which is good. No sign of severe infection in the blood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the sputum test?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We sent a sample today. Preliminary results show normal mouth bacteria—no fungus or dangerous germs yet. But we’ll keep the fluconazole just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a yeast infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No fungus was isolated, but since you had plaques before, we’re being cautious. The fluconazole will help prevent it from coming back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I understand. What’s the plan now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you overnight for IV antibiotics and monitoring. The pulmonary team will review your case tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be here long?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely just one night. If you improve, we can set you up with home IV therapy so you finish the course safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in. How are you feeling after the first dose of IV antibiotic?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I think I’m breathing a little easier. Still some mucus, but not as much struggle.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great progress. Keep using your nebulizers as scheduled. We’ll repeat the sputum culture before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. The pulmonary team reviewed your case. They agree with continuing IV ceftriaxone for 10 days and fluconazole for 5.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’ll be on IV meds at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. A nurse will teach you how to give the IV dose safely. It’s once a day, so it’s manageable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the other new pill—azithromycin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s for additional coverage against bronchitis or tracheitis. Four-day course, one pill a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m still on my regular meds too, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—albuterol, ipratropium, omeprazole, ranitidine, Singulair, and fluoxetine. We’re keeping everything consistent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t want to mess up my routine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat sputum culture came back. Still shows normal respiratory flora—no concerning bacteria or fungus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no new infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not that we can see. But since your symptoms are real and similar to last time, we’re treating it as a recurrence of tracheitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I just want to get back on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to discharge you today. You’ll take ceftriaxone IV at home for 8 more days, azithromycin for 4, and fluconazole for 5.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow up with my pulmonologist?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. They’ll see you soon. Keep using your nebulizers, stay hydrated, and suction as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’re glad you’re improving. A nurse will go over your IV instructions before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final check-in. You’re doing well—clear lungs, stable vitals. You’re cleared to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. I’ll make sure to take everything as directed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, especially the IV antibiotic. If you have fever, increased secretions, or trouble breathing, call your doctor or come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing a great job managing your health. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Quick call to confirm—you got home okay and started your IV antibiotic?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, Doctor. I’m all set. Nurse came by and showed me everything. First dose is done.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Keep up the good work. Call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last message: blood cultures are still pending, but no growth so far. That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. I feel safer hearing that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring everything. Finish your meds and keep your follow-up. You’re on the right track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for all your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care and breathe easy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final note: your discharge summary is complete. You’re officially discharged as of now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll follow all the instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re confident you will. Talk to you soon.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with a history of tracheobronchomalacia, bronchopulmonary dysplasia, and chronic bronchitis was admitted due to increased green sputum production, difficulty clearing tracheal secretions, and worsening shortness of breath, similar to a recent hospitalization. She had been on oral cefuroxime and fluconazole but was not improving. IV ceftriaxone was started, and she showed clinical improvement overnight. A sputum culture showed only commensal flora, and no fungal growth was detected. The pulmonary team recommended completing a 10-day course of IV ceftriaxone and oral fluconazole, along with a 4-day course of azithromycin. She was discharged home with home IV antibiotic therapy, clear instructions, and a plan for follow-up with her pulmonologist.
